When stocks and bonds fall in the same year: a balanced fund through rising rates and high inflation

Break a balanced fund’s bad year into its stock loss, bond income, bond price fall and lost purchasing power, then follow how a higher bond yield works afterwards and how long the real value takes to come back.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Test a balanced fund in a year when stocks fall, bond yields rise and inflation jumps

Interactive planning lab

A $100,000 fund holds 60% stocks and 40% bonds, rebalanced each year-end. In the shock year stocks fall 12% and bond yields rise 2 percentage points from 1.5%, so a bond sleeve with 7 years of duration returns about -12.5% (yield less duration × rise). Afterwards stocks return 6% and bonds earn the new 3.5% yield each year. Inflation is 6.3% in the shock year and 2.5% later. Fees are assumed to be inside the returns; tax, contributions and withdrawals are not modeled. Every return is a hypothetical input, not a forecast or the record of any fund.

The central idea

Bonds usually cushion a stock decline, but when inflation forces interest rates up, bond prices can fall at the same time. The same higher yields then raise the bond sleeve’s later income, so the damage is partly repaid over roughly the bond fund’s duration. Purchasing power, not the nominal balance, is the measure that recovers last.

01

The year the cushion did not cushion

A balanced fund holds stocks and bonds together so that a bad year for one is softened by the other. Most of the time that works: when stocks fall because the economy weakens, interest rates often fall too, and bond prices rise. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor site notes the limit of that idea: diversification provides reasonable protection in normal markets but becomes less effective in extreme conditions, when the prices of most investments can drop together.

A different kind of bad year arrives when inflation is the problem. Central banks raise rates to slow prices, bond yields rise, and the prices of bonds already held fall at the same time as stocks. For a balanced-fund investor this year can feel worse than a larger stock crash, because the part of the portfolio that was supposed to be safe is also down, and the money that remains buys less.

This guide splits such a year into its parts, then follows what happens afterwards. It does not predict when the next one will come.

02

What the official data show for 2022

The first chart plots three dated series for Canada. Consumer price inflation, measured by Statistics Canada as the 12-month change in the all-items CPI, rose from 4.8% in December 2021 to a peak of 8.1% in June 2022. The Bank of Canada raised its target for the overnight rate from 0.25% in early 2022 to 4.25% by December 2022 and 5% by July 2023. The Government of Canada 10-year benchmark bond yield ended December 2021 at 1.42% and December 2022 at 3.30%, a rise of almost two percentage points in one year.

By September 2026 the latest observations were 3.1% inflation, a 2.25% policy rate and a 3.99% 10-year yield. These are dated readings, not a forecast. The chart does not show any fund’s return; the model below uses its own editable assumptions so that each effect can be seen on its own.

03

Splitting the shock year into four pieces

The default fund starts at CAD 100,000 with 60% in stocks and 40% in bonds. In the shock year stocks fall 12%. Bond yields start at 1.5% and rise by 2 percentage points, and the bond sleeve has a duration of 7 years. Duration is a measure of interest-rate sensitivity: a bond fund with a duration of 7 loses roughly 7% of its value for each 1-point rise in yields. Inflation is 6.3% in the shock year.

  • Stocks: 12% of CAD 60,000 is a loss of CAD 7,200.
  • Bond income: 1.5% on CAD 40,000 adds CAD 600.
  • Bond prices: 7 × 2 points = 14% of CAD 40,000, a loss of CAD 5,600. The bond sleeve returns about −12.5%, almost the same as stocks.
  • Inflation: the fund ends the year at CAD 87,800, a −12.2% return, but after 6.3% inflation that buys what about CAD 82,596 bought at the start. The real loss is about 17.4%.

If yields had not risen, the same stock fall would have left the fund at CAD 93,400, down 6.6%. The rate rise alone cost CAD 5,600 in the shock year. The duration rule is a first-order estimate; for large yield moves the actual loss on a bond is somewhat smaller because of convexity, explained in the bond convexity guide.

04

Higher yields are the part of the damage that pays back

The loss on bonds from rising yields has a second side. After the shock, the bond sleeve earns 3.5% a year instead of 1.5%. In the third chart, the fund that went through the rate rise trails the no-rise version by CAD 5,600 after year one, then closes the gap each year and passes it in year 10. After 15 years it is worth about CAD 173,838 against about CAD 166,148 for the fund whose yields never rose.

The catch-up time is close to the bond sleeve’s duration, which is no coincidence: duration is also roughly the holding period over which a yield change’s price effect and its income effect balance out. The bond reinvestment guide shows that mechanism for a single bond. Two caveats matter. The model holds the new yield constant, while real yields keep moving. And it gives every duration the same yield, while longer bonds often, but not always, pay more; a short-duration bond fund is not simply a better version of a long one.

05

Purchasing power is what recovers last

The real concern for most savers is not the nominal balance but what it will buy. In the default case the fund is back above CAD 100,000 in nominal terms in year 4, but in start-year dollars it regains CAD 100,000 only in year 9. After 15 years it is worth about CAD 115,738 in start-year dollars. Inflation in the shock year is a permanent step up in the price level: prices do not fall back when inflation slows, they just rise more slowly, as the inflation and purchasing power guide explains.

The heatmap repeats the calculation for stock shares from 20% to 100% and stock falls from 0% to 40%, keeping the entered rate rise and inflation. Two patterns stand out:

  • With no stock fall at all, a 20% stock fund takes until year 13 to regain its real value, while a 100% stock fund takes until year 3. In a pure rate-and-inflation shock, the bond-heavy fund is the one that suffers.
  • With a 40% stock fall, every mix needs 18 or 19 years. The balanced structure still spreads risk, but the usual ranking of “more bonds, less loss” is weaker when both assets fall together.

These counts are arithmetic results for one set of constant later returns. Markets have historically recovered from declines, but the OSC cautions that this can take months or several years; no recovery date is guaranteed.

06

Responding to the worry without abandoning the plan

  1. Separate the money by when it is needed. Spending planned within a few years belongs in savings or short-term deposits whose value does not depend on bond prices. Money for goals ten or more years away can usually ride out the shock year described here.
  2. Look at the bond sleeve’s duration. Fund Facts and the fund’s reports describe the bond holdings. A longer duration means a larger price fall when yields rise, and a larger benefit when they fall.
  3. Keep contributions going from your paycheque. New money invested after a rate rise buys bonds at the higher yield and stocks at lower prices; FINRA describes dollar-cost averaging as a way to reduce the impact of a decline on purchases, without protecting money already invested. Moving an existing lump sum into the fund in stages is a different decision, compared in the phased-investing guide.
  4. Keep the account rules separate from the fund. A balanced fund in a TFSA or RRSP has no tax on its rebalancing; the same fund in a non-registered account distributes taxable income and gains. The account changes the tax, not the market risk.
  5. Check the mix against the loss you can live through. The risk-profile stress test turns a stock share into dollars. Choosing a lower-risk mix once, deliberately, differs from switching to cash after a bad year, which the crash-warning guide tests.
